Hour 3 of The Clay Travis & Buck Sexton Show opens with an in-depth conversation about DOGE, Elon Musk, federal government spending, waste, fraud, the national debt and government efficiency. Clay and Buck welcome Tyler Hassen, former acting assistant secretary at the U.S. Department of the Interior, former senior DOGE official and author of Inside DOGE: The Real Story from a Senior Insider. Hassen offers his firsthand account of working with Musk’s DOGE team and argues that waste inside the federal government is substantially worse than most Americans realize. He discusses DOGE’s reported savings, efforts to increase accountability for federal contracts and grants, and an initiative designed to improve information attached to trillions of dollars in Treasury payments. Drawing on his experience at the Interior Department, Hassen describes finding federal contracts for projects such as groundwater assessments in Mauritania that officials struggled to justify, while explaining the DOGE philosophy of forcing agencies to “defend the spend.”
The Hour 3 DOGE interview expands into the larger challenge of America’s roughly $40 trillion national debt, growing federal budgets and rapidly increasing interest costs. Clay, Buck and Hassen debate whether Washington has a revenue problem or a spending problem and whether economic growth alone can prevent the debt from becoming unsustainable. Hassen argues that government needs more entrepreneurs, engineers, lawyers and private-sector leaders willing to spend one or two years in public service, calling for an elite, bipartisan effort that continues across presidential administrations. He also discusses fraud in federal programs, federal grants flowing through state governments, Medicaid and Social Security, and praises efforts to trace where taxpayer dollars ultimately go. His proposed philosophy is to not merely “drain the swamp” but to “flood it with talent.” He also describes working late into the night with Elon Musk, discusses DOGE engineers facing intense public criticism and threats, and praises their efforts to modernize antiquated federal technology systems.
Hassen also identifies Congress as a major obstacle to federal spending reductions, recounting how Interior sought a substantial budget reduction only to encounter congressional resistance. He discusses a multibillion-dollar rescission package while arguing that substantially more spending restraint is necessary. The conversation examines the sheer complexity of the federal bureaucracy, the difficulty of determining who is accountable for individual expenditures and the outdated IT infrastructure within government agencies. Hassen nevertheless says he believes the national debt can ultimately be addressed if Washington commits enough time and capable people to the task. The interview concludes on a lighter note as Hassen, who has known Buck since childhood, recalls their school days, academic competition and dodgeball games before discussing his new book and his goal of presenting an insider’s account of DOGE.
Hour 3 then pivots to President Donald Trump, CNN, MSNBC and Politico, with Clay and Buck discussing Trump’s decision to exclude certain news organizations from covering some of his events. Clay predicts the dispute could ultimately produce a court fight over press access. The hosts use the controversy to examine the changing American media landscape, arguing that X, formerly Twitter, has expanded the marketplace of political ideas while the Washington Post, CNN and CBS News have begun providing a broader range of viewpoints than in previous election cycles. Clay argues that these changes could have major consequences for the 2028 presidential election and political media narratives, particularly if CNN becomes less ideologically predictable. Buck notes CNN’s increasing willingness to feature pro-Trump commentators and contrasts that with what he characterizes as the network’s approach during earlier stages of the Trump era.
Clay and Buck then play comments from President Trump explaining his criticism of CNN and MSNBC, his complaints about persistently negative coverage and his contention that news organizations have an obligation to be fair. Trump also points to his administration’s economic and foreign-policy record while defending decisions restricting access for outlets he considers unfair. The hosts discuss whether presidents and other government officials inevitably make subjective choices about which journalists receive access and note that, although the controversy has generated significant concern within the media industry, they believe it has attracted comparatively little attention from the broader public.
A major portion of Hour 3 of Clay and Buck returns to public education, parental involvement, classroom discipline and school culture. Responding to listener feedback, Buck argues that successful schools depend heavily on parents who reinforce respect for teachers, rules, order and education at home. The hosts discuss the difficulties public-school teachers face when dealing with disruptive students and school fights, including concerns that educators may hesitate to physically separate fighting students because of liability and disciplinary policies. They also discuss federal education policy and disagreements over whether racial disparities in school discipline should be treated as evidence of discriminatory disciplinary practices. Their broader argument is that school discipline, parental expectations and peer culture can matter as much as, or more than, additional education spending.
That discussion leads to one of the hour’s most extended and humorous exchanges: corporal punishment and paddling in American public schools. Clay recounts growing up around Nashville public schools where students could be paddled for serious misbehavior, stunning Buck, who says such practices were completely foreign to his New York City upbringing. The hosts discuss the differences between Southern and Northeastern school culture, the historical use of paddles and “switches,” visits to the principal’s office and the deterrent effect Clay remembers corporal punishment having on classroom behavior. Their production team reports during the program that public-school corporal punishment remains legally permissible in a number of states, which prompts Buck to express disbelief that the practice can still legally exist in parts of the United States. Listeners subsequently send their own stories about paddling by teachers, principals and Catholic-school nuns, including accounts from Michigan, Ohio and Southern California.
The education conversation also returns to the significance of peer groups, private schools and family culture. Clay argues that many parents who can afford private education are purchasing not merely classroom instruction but access to a peer environment built around stronger academic and behavioral expectations. He invokes former Notre Dame football coach Lou Holtz to make the larger point that parents have a limited window to establish values before teenagers become increasingly influenced by their friends. Clay and Buck suggest that the behavior and expectations of classmates can have major consequences for an individual child’s educational experience, reinforcing their wider theme that culture within schools cannot simply be repaired by increasing budgets.
Sports also enters Hour 3 when Clay delivers disappointing news for New York Giants fans about quarterback Jaxson Dart, saying reports indicate the knee injury Dart suffered against Los Angeles could potentially end his season. Because Dart had previously introduced President Trump at a rally, Clay predicts that some political opponents online will celebrate his injury, tying sports back into the program’s recurring examination of political polarization and social-media behavior. Buck jokes that Clay has effectively “paddled” Giants fans across the New York tri-state area with the news.
Finally, Hour 3 of The Clay Travis & Buck Sexton Show closes with a brief look toward the 2026 midterm elections. Clay reports that Kamala Harris has arrived in Michigan to campaign alongside Abdul El-Sayed and says he hopes her return to a public campaign setting will generate new audio and provide another indicator of Democratic messaging heading into November. The program ends with additional listener memories about school paddling and discipline, bringing the hour full circle from the enormous institutional challenge of controlling federal spending to the equally spirited debate over controlling behavior in American classrooms.

The White House has a list of stories it says are biased, even dangerous, enough to warrant banishment of those outlets from the credentialed press there. How false were they? Read for yourself.
Three media titans are due back in court Wednesday to convince a federal judge their press credentials and access to the White House should be restored. The Justice Department has named specific articles CNN, MS Now and Politico have published in the past year for the revocations.
Download the Straight Arrow app today to get the stories that matter free from manipulation, bias or agenda.™
Point phone camera here
Lawyers with the Justice Department argued in court papers that CNN, MS Now and Politico each have published articles that threaten national security or “spread falsehoods,” according to letters sent to each organization. Michael Velchik, senior counsel for the civil rights division, argued that President Donald Trump has the executive duty to revoke credentials for places and journalists that interfere with government operations.
Velchik’s reasoning clashes with Trump’s own, where he claimed on Truth Social it was due to their “constant ‘reporting’ fake news.”
“After all, access to the White House is a privilege—not a right,” Velchik wrote.
The three news organizations haven’t responded to Velchik’s claims outside of the Washington, D.C. courtroom.
A coalition of 51 news organizations and affinity groups filed a Friend-of-the-Court brief Wednesday supporting the trio’s request for a temporary restraining order. Among the group is ABC News, CBS News, NBC Universal, Fox News, The Guardian, McClatchy Media Group, The Associated Press, Minnesota Public Radio and Reuters.
“The administration’s rationalization for its conduct provides all the evidence needed to demonstrate that its expulsion of journalists is illegal and unconstitutional under controlling precedent,” they wrote.
Media law and press freedom advocates have said the Justice Department is misinterpreting the law.
“The Pentagon Papers case rejected a prior restraint aimed at specific documents claimed to pose national security risks,” the Freedom of the Press Foundation wrote on X Wednesday. “Anyone who argues ’national security’ are magic words justifying banning news outlets should be laughed out of court and sanctioned.”
Access is disputed, but media lawyers have urged journalists to always exercise caution when publishing classified material, since they can be prosecuted for disseminating such documents, according to the First Amendment Institute at Middle Tennessee State University.
Two of the most famous cases with First Amendment exemptions involve Julian Assange, the founder of WikiLeaks, and Edward Snowden, a former National Security Agency administrator with top-level security clearance.
Assange pleaded guilty in 2024 to publishing military secrets, which federal prosecutors initially said violated the Espionage Act, according to The Associated Press. Snowden was accused of leaking classified information to The Guardian and The Washington Post in 2013 and charged under the Espionage Act as well. He lives in exile in Russia.
“News outlets publish classified or ‘sensitive’ information every day,” the free press organization said on X. “If that’s the standard, Trump could ban any reporter at any time. Journalists must refuse to be intimidated. Publish even more about every news story this White House wants buried.”
Investigations into a journalist, Iran War
Velchik listed 11 articles he argued validated Trump’s right to revoke CNN, MS Now and Politico’s access to the White House. The majority of the stories focused on the Pentagon and where the Department of Defense stood in the Iran War.
He listed one published on Aug. 6 by MS Now, where the television network reported concerns military officials expressed to other media about the nation’s weapons stockpile. The network followed up, stating that the Iran War further depleted supply.
MS Now didn’t indicate in the story that it received information directly from sources with top-level security clearances, nor did it grant anonymity requests because the information was confidential. Instead, the story relied on combining articles across the media landscape on the Trump administration’s military supply.
In Politico’s case, Velchik pointed to a story the publication exclusively ran in April 2025 where five anonymous sources said that the White House debated easing sanctions on Russia. Politico granted the sources anonymity and reached out to the White House, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and special envoy Steve Witkoff for comment on the story, which all three provided.
For CNN, Velchik’s claim is more targeted at the publication’s access to sources that have provided “top-secret” and military information. The first centered on an exclusive about Trump’s plans to restore the White House bunker under the East Wing, which CNN attributed the “top secret” phrase to White House Historical Association historian Bill Seale.
“Publication of sensitive security information, and misinformation about national security information, diverts White House resources and those of the national security team in particular, which must evaluate whether the leaked information is classified, the source of any leak, and the security implications of any such disclosure,” Velchik wrote in court papers. ”The spread of misinformation, especially relating to national security, is a threat that undermines the President’s ability to safeguard the national security.”

US judge leaves White House media ban in place for now
The news organisations are scheduled to make their case to a US district judge on Wednesday afternoon.
US President Donald Trump’s administration has defended his decision to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House grounds, arguing in a court filing that the president has broad authority to determine which journalists can access the complex and that the outlets’ reporting raised national security concerns.
US District Judge Timothy Kelly held the hearing in Washington to consider a request by the news outlets for a temporary restraining order that would immediately reinstate their White House access while a legal challenge they filed on Monday plays out. He did not make a ruling, and it was unclear when he would issue a decision.

In a filing ahead of the hearing, Justice Department lawyers said the outlets had failed to meet what the administration described as standards of professionalism and decorum.
“Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” the filing said.
The White House press office sent letters to the three outlets on Tuesday alleging their coverage involved “trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information”.
The letters, filed in court, cited CNN publishing “top-secret” construction details of a bunker beneath the White House’s East Wing, MS NOW coverage of the impact of the Iran war on US military munitions and a Politico report about funding for the White House ballroom that included details about Secret Service security improvements. It also cited Politico relying on anonymous sources for a report describing the Republican congressional midterm convention as a “disaster”.
The filing argues that publishing such information can divert national security personnel and resources as officials assess whether material is classified and determine its security implications.
The administration is also asking the court to overturn a 1977 appeals court ruling, Sherrill vs Knight, which held that White House press access could not be denied arbitrarily or without compelling reasons.
The lawsuit by the three outlets argues that the ban violates their First Amendment rights.
The proceedings are historic, said Katie Fallow, deputy litigation director at the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University.
“No president has taken this explicit of a step” to ban entire news outlets because he doesn’t like their reporting, she said. “There have been various presidents throughout history who have grumbled about the press or threatened to take more major steps, but really there was nothing at this level before Trump.”
The case was assigned to District Judge Kelly, who previously ordered the restoration of CNN reporter Jim Acosta’s White House credentials during Trump’s first term. Despite Kelly being a Trump-appointed judge, the president has already expressed his disappointment in the selection.
“They have drawn a great Judge, for them, a man who ruled in favor of Jim Acosta, who now seems to have disappeared from the Planet. The Judge’s name is Tim Kelly, and he was, sadly, appointed by ‘TRUMP,’” the president wrote on Truth Social. “In other words, almost without question and, as usual, we’ll go for appeal because Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown ‘sources,’ shouldn’t be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World.”
An amicus brief was filed by other news groups Wednesday, urging the court to immediately restore White House access to the three outlets. It said, “the targeted expulsion of news media from White House grounds injures the public interest” and that “unassailable First Amendment law makes any viewpoint-based decision to bar reporters from a nonpublic forum constitutionally repugnant”.

The United States Justice Department has requested that a federal judge dismiss the emergency application submitted by CNN, Politico, and MS NOW to get their reporters readmitted to the White House.
In a court document filed on Tuesday evening, the government’s lawyers justified President Donald Trump’s decision to ban the three organizations. They stated that access to the building is a privilege, not a right.
The lawyers also stated that the outlets had published classified or sensitive information, which is why the ban relates to national security; furthermore, they argued that a court order lifting the ban could raise separation-of-powers concerns, as reported by Bloomberg News.
The context is that on Monday, the three outlets filed a lawsuit against Trump. They claim that he is retaliating against them for the way they have reported the news, an action which violates the First Amendment protection of a free press.
They also assert that the ban came into effect without any prior notice or opportunity to challenge it, contrary to their Fifth Amendment right to due process.
“This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the outlets said in their lawsuit.
The government’s argument extends to those three news organizations. As stated by ABC News, the department wants the president to consider journalists’ views when granting access and has also requested that a landmark ruling safeguarding reporters’ access be set aside.
As quoted by CNN, the department stated that at the very least the government might control reporters’ access to restricted presidential areas, such as the Oval Office, on the grounds of viewpoint discrimination.
The document contains letters sent by the White House Press Office to each of the organizations in question.
These letters allege that all three have violated the standards of professionalism and decorum and have spread false claims regarding national security.
The letters refer to particular stories, such as reports on the war in Iran, coverage of Trump’s White House ballroom, and sanctions on Russia according to Bloomberg.
They also mention a Politico Playbook report about the Republican midterm convention in Dallas and an MS NOW report from August concerning the munitions used by the United States in the Iran conflict.
The letters, however, are dated September 22, four days after Trump announced the ban on Truth Social. At that point, the reporters Betsy Klein, Cheyenne Haslett and Akayla Gardner had already been turned away at the gates.
The media outlets now have until 5 p.m. on Friday, September 25, to respond or the decision will become final.
At the same time, over 40 media companies and press organizations, including NBCUniversal, the owner of NBC News, have submitted a brief in support of the banned outlets, NBC News stated.
The major television networks have also halted their live broadcasts of Trump since the ban came into effect.
The ban comes after Trump has already imposed restrictions on journalists, such as the 2025 limitation on the Associated Press, which was also decided by the same court.
This year, the United States dropped to 64th place in the RSF press freedom index, its lowest-ever ranking. Moreover, press freedom organizations have taken legal action against Trump for his paid Truth Social feed.
Trump first called the policy “the ban on the free press”, but on Monday said it targeted fake news rather than press freedom.
Timothy Kelly, who was appointed to the position by Trump, will consider the outlets’ application for a temporary restraining order on Wednesday afternoon.
In 2018, Judge Kelly had instructed the White House to reinstate the press pass for CNN correspondent Jim Acosta, and Trump has stated that he will appeal any decision against him.

The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) submitted a legal filing on Tuesday arguing that President Donald Trump has the right to ban media outlets from the White House, dubiously citing issues of “national security.”
Trump announced the ban — which affects CNN, MS NOW, and Politico — in a Truth Social post on Friday, claiming he was banning the outlets as a “result of their constant ‘reporting’ [of] FAKE NEWS!”
Notably, Trump has a long history of describing reporting that portrays him in a negative light as “fake,” even when the reporting is factual.
In a subsequent post over the weekend, Trump again alleged that the news agencies utilized fake reports, claiming that such reporting is “a threat to our National Security” that “must be stopped.”
Trump’s posts were cited by the DOJ in a legal filing responding to a joint lawsuit from CNN, MS NOW, and Politico. The suit seeks to put a stay on Trump’s attempt to block their access to the White House.
The DOJ argues that such access is a “privilege” that news agencies enjoy, and states that presidents have the legal authority to block whoever they want.
“Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” the DOJ filing forcefully claims, adding that Trump can enforce “minimum standards for bona fide journalists and safeguarding national security information.”
The filing also argues that these news orgs were unprofessional through their use of anonymous sources to publish stories about the White House — a practice that has existed for decades, if not longer, and which Trump himself has utilized in the past to criticize his political opponents.
Attempting to prove Trump’s order should remain in place, the filing cites CNN’s reporting on a bunker underneath Trump’s planned East Wing ballroom; MS NOW’s reporting on the White House’s investigation into leaks; and Politico’s reporting on Secret Service funds being used to help pay for security improvements in the planned ballroom.
It is unclear how the outlets’ reporting on these subjects detrimentally affects national security — indeed, the reports contain information that the American public may have a vested interest in. Observers also noted that some of the reports cited in the filing are a matter of public record.
Ryan Goodman, co-editor-in-chief of Just Security, described the reporting cited in the filing as “core First Amendment protected reporting.”
The DOJ “gives an example of ‘In August 2026, MSNOW claimed that the Iran conflict had ‘significantly depleted’ the US military’s munitions supply.’ What was the MSNOW source for that claim? This document, which is published in the Federal Register,” Goodman wrote, sharing the document in his Bluesky post.
Earlier on Tuesday, Trump attacked members of the press at the United Nations, where he was set to give a speech. When CNN’s Kaitlan Collins tried to ask the president about the war in Iran, he responded: “I’m surprised CNN is here is covering me. You shouldn’t be here.”
“The United Nations allowed us in, sir,” Collins retorted.
“You should not be here covering me,” Trump said. He then wrongly claimed that the network had said it would no longer be reporting on him due to the ban.
Late on Tuesday night — just after the DOJ submitted its response to the joint lawsuit from the news organizations — Trump posted another attack against Collins on Truth Social.
“All of the SLEAZEBAGS, like Third Rate ‘Reporter,’ Kaitlan Collins, of Fake News CNN, a truly unhappy person, said they weren’t going to be covering me,” Trump wrote. “Then why were they ranting and raving like Lunatics, in the Press Area, at the United Nations?”
“Why was she there?” Trump added.
Americans largely oppose Trump’s attempt to keep press he doesn’t like out of the White House.
An Economist/YouGov poll published on Tuesday showed respondents the president’s initial Truth Social post announcing the White House ban on CNN, MS NOW, and Politico. Only 32 percent said they approved of the ban, while 58 percent disapproved — including nearly 1 in 2 Americans (49 percent) who said they “strongly disapproved.”

Trump White House ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico faces First Amendment test
A Washington court is hearing arguments on Trump's ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. The case could decide whether the administration's security rationale overrides press freedom protections.
A court in Washington is set to hear arguments on Wednesday in a case over US President Donald Trump's decision to bar CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House grounds. The three outlets have sued, saying the move violates the First Amendment, while the administration says it has the authority to decide who is allowed into the White House.
In a court filing late Tuesday, the administration said, "Access to the White House is a privilege - not a right," and argued that the reporting of the three organisations posed a threat to national security. Trump had earlier focused on what he called negative coverage and "fake news", but on Tuesday he also began stressing the national security argument.
The filing said the ban did not violate the constitutional guarantee of a free press. Administration lawyers argued that the outlets had breached the "standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House complex, including by trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues and publishing sensitive or classified information".
The administration said letters sent to each outlet listed "a non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents, including those that have threatened national security and spread falsehoods". Among the examples cited were CNN's report on "top-secret" construction details related to the East Wing bunker, MS NOW's report on "an alleged leak investigation", and Politico's publication of "a document detailing funding for the White House ballroom containing intricate descriptions of how the Secret Service would invest in security improvements".
Politico's letter, the filing said, listed six reporting incidents, including a June report that quoted a "senior administration official ... granted anonymity" on whether a preliminary deal would end the conflict with Iran. That appeared to refer to a background briefing arranged by the White House itself, where an official spoke to reporters on condition of anonymity under White House ground rules. Several other outlets also reported the remarks.
Trump defended the ban at the United Nations on Tuesday, saying, "I think we have a right to clean out fake news." The ban was announced on Friday, and the next day journalists from the three outlets found that their entry badges had been disabled. On Monday, the outlets filed a joint lawsuit alleging they were singled out because of the content of their coverage, calling it a "blatant violation" of the First Amendment and asking the court to restore their access immediately.
Other media organisations also responded. The five-network US television press pool, of which CNN is a member, decided to suspend coverage of Trump's events until further notice. The Associated Press also joined a group of organisations that did not publish photographs of the president on Monday. On Wednesday, the network pool was again absent from the daily White House press schedule.
The ban and the lawsuit come amid a long-running conflict between Trump and media organisations he sees as unfavourable, especially in his second term. The administration's court filing also used historical examples to argue that presidents can decide which reporters receive favourable treatment. It said President Theodore Roosevelt invited reporters into the Oval Office for off-the-record briefings during his midday shave and used the sessions to reward and punish journalists, while President John F Kennedy gave certain correspondents special access and advance notice of announcements.
At the heart of Wednesday's hearing is whether the White House can bar the three outlets from its grounds on the grounds cited by the administration, or whether the move amounts to unconstitutional discrimination based on their reporting and viewpoint.
